strong-stage1:
You are writing a task model for someone using a website through an AI agent. The first step is the task tree: a hierarchical task analysis of how a person actually does the task, before any validation questions get attached.

<<EXEMPLAR_TREE>>

Read how they are built:
- ids are outline numbers ("1", "1.2", "1.2.1"). The root is "0".
- labels are short doing-phrases ("Search for sandals", "Read the price"), five words or fewer where possible.
- a note says the thing about that step that is not obvious from the label - why the step exists, what makes it tricky, what a person actually does there. notes are lowercase, plain, one or two sentences. not every node needs one.
- every node with children has a plan sentence saying the order they run in, in this exact style: "do 1, then 2. if the sandal fails a check, repeat 2 with another. if none are left, repeat 1."
- include the recovery paths (fixing errors, going back for another candidate, undoing, cancelling), not just the happy path.
- cover the whole task, from first search to having proof it worked.

## How big the tree has to be

Measure the trees above before you write. They run <<NODE_LO>> to <<NODE_HI>> nodes, with <<LEAF_LO>> to <<LEAF_HI>> leaves, under <<TOP_LO>> to <<TOP_HI>> top-level phases, and they go <<DEPTH>> levels deep including the root.

A tree that comes out around half that size has not been decomposed far enough. That is the single most common way this step fails, so check your draft against the numbers before you answer.

Two rules that get you there:

1. **A leaf is one check or one action, performed in one moment.** "Read the result count" is a leaf. "Handle the results" is not. If a leaf's label contains "and", or names a whole screen, or would take a person more than a few seconds, split it.
2. **A phase with only one or two steps under it is usually a phase you have not opened yet.** Go back and say what a person actually does inside it, in order.

## The phases a first draft leaves out

Read across the trees above and notice what they all carry that a first draft would not. Every one of them has phases before and after the obvious middle:

- getting into the right state to start at all - the right account, the right site, the right region, the right version of the thing
- what happens between deciding and committing - the review step, the terms, the money
- proof it worked, after the commit - the confirmation, the record, the email, the number to quote later
- the way back out - cancelling, undoing, changing, and when that stops being possible
- keeping it working afterwards, where the task has an afterwards

Do not add a phase that this task does not have. Do check each of these against the task and open the ones it does have.

## The checking is part of the task, not a layer on top of it

The person is not only getting the task done. They are satisfying themselves that
it was done right, and that is most of what this model is for. So the tree has to
contain the places where a careful person stops and checks, as nodes in their own
right - not only the steps that move the task forward.

This is the single biggest way a tree written from a request goes wrong. A request
says what someone wants ("when was the tower finished, check wikipedia", "find me
sandals under $40"). Written straight down, that produces a tree of getting the
answer: search, open, read off the value, done. A person doing it for real also
asks whether the source can be trusted, whether the thing in front of them is the
thing they asked for, and whether what just happened actually took effect - and
none of that is in the request, because nobody says it out loud.

Read the trees above again for this specifically. They carry nodes for judging a
source, for reading what you are agreeing to, for confirming an action landed, and
for the ways back out. Those nodes are why the model is worth having. A tree whose
leaves are all "do the next step" cannot host a single useful question, because
there is nothing at those leaves that a person would check.

## Now build the tree

<<QUERY>>

Split the request into "task" (a plain one-line naming of the task) and "ask" (the specific constraints the person gave, as a short comma-separated phrase like "flat, a strap behind the heel, girls size 5, under $40").

You have not seen the actual website yet. Where the tree depends on how the site actually works - what filters exist, what the checkout steps are, what a results page shows - build your best guess from how sites of this kind normally work, and mark the node with "needsInterfaceCheck": a short phrase saying what to confirm against the real interface (for example "check what the results page actually shows"). Mark only the nodes where the real interface could change the structure, not every node.

Answer with only JSON, no prose around it, in this shape:
{"task": "...", "ask": "...", "tree": {"id": "0", "label": "...", "note": "...", "plan": "...", "children": [{"id": "1", "label": "...", "needsInterfaceCheck": "...", "children": [...]}, ...]}}

One rule above all others: the tree may only commit to what the ask commits to.
Anything the ask does not specify - a seat, insurance, bags, an airline, a
payment method - is a DECISION NODE for the person, never a default step. Name
such nodes by the decision ("Handle seat selection"), never by an assumed
outcome ("Skip seat selection"). The person who said nothing about seats has
not said no to seats.
strong-questions:
You are writing the validation questions for a task model - the questions a person would want answered while an AI agent does the task for them in a browser. Each question marks a decision point: a moment where the person would look at the page and check something before things move on.

<<EXEMPLAR>>

What to copy from them:
- questions are short and concrete, in the voice of the person glancing at the page: "How many results?", "Is size 5 in stock?", "Which card pays?". Never "verify the result count" or "confirm stock availability".
- each question sits on the leaf node where that check happens.
- "why" says in plain words why a person would want this answered - what the answer tells them, and what goes wrong if nobody looks. one or two sentences, lowercase.
- "whatTheAgentLoses" says what happens to this signal when an agent does the step instead of the person: does it reach them at all, and in what form (a spoken report, nothing, a claim they cannot check). this task has no recorded agent run, so write what a typical agent run would lose - the default is that the agent sees the page and the person gets at most a line in a spoken report.
- cover the unrequested checks too: quality judgments nobody asked for (ratings, reviews), what the person is agreeing to (fees, dates, cancellation terms), whether actions actually landed (confirmations, receipts), and the ways out (cancel, undo, change).
- questions ask what the page shows or what the person decides, never "did the agent do X correctly".

## How many questions per leaf

Look at the exemplar models: every leaf in them carries at least one question. That is the shape to match.

Work leaf by leaf and decide for that leaf alone:

- **one question** is the normal case. The step has one thing a person checks.
- **two questions** where the leaf holds two genuinely separate checks - two different facts, read at the same moment, that could each be wrong on their own and that the person would react to differently. "What does it cost?" and "Does the price include the fees?" are two. "What does it cost?" and "Is the price right?" are one.
- **three** only where the step is a dense screen and each of the three is a distinct decision. This should be rare.
- **none** only where there is genuinely nothing to check, and then say so in the leaf's note.

Do not aim for a number of questions across the model. There is no target. A model that reaches a count by writing questions nobody would ask is worse than a short one, and it is obvious on reading: the giveaway is a question whose answer could not change what the person does next.

Before you write a second question on a leaf, say to yourself what the person does differently depending on each answer. If the two answers lead to the same next move, it is one question.

## The task

Task: <<TASK>>
Ask: <<ASK>>

Here is the whole tree, for context:

<<TREE>>

Write questions for these leaves only:

<<SCOPE>>

Answer with only JSON, no prose around it: a list with one entry per leaf in the scope list that gets questions (leave out the ones that get none):
[{"nodeId": "1.2", "questions": [{"question": "...", "why": "...", "whatTheAgentLoses": "..."}]}]

Where the tree meets something the ask never specified (seats, insurance,
bags, upsells), the question is the person's choice ("Do you want a seat
pick?"), not a check that an assumed skip happened.
strong-coding:
The task is: <<TASK>>
What the person asked for: <<ASK>>

Both of those decide the codings below. A moment is when an answer is wanted
relative to THIS task's run, and whether a step is hard to undo depends
entirely on what the task is - paying for something and reading an article have
nothing in common there. Code against this task, not against what the question
sounds like in general.

You are coding the validation questions of a task model. Each question gets four things: a cluster (which interface type it is), a moment (when it fires relative to the agent's run), a paradigm (which shape the widget draws, a number 1 to 12), and one example widget (what the interface would actually say, what it needs to read off the page, and what the user can do about it).

Here are the interface types:

<<TYPE_CARDS>>

The moments:
- "Now": pause agent execution
- "After": after agent execution, show modified world state without pausing agent
- "Completion": after the agent fully completes, show final world state
- "On demand": user can interrupt agent execution at any time

Here are the paradigms:

<<PARADIGM_CARDS>>

<<EXEMPLAR>>

What to copy:
- cluster comes from the cards. Propose a new type ONLY if none of them fit. A new type needs a full card in the same format - what it is, when it applies, the option pair, a worked example from this task - plus one sentence on why none of the existing ones fit. A new type without a full card gets rejected.
- moment is decided per question, not per type. an approve question is usually "Now"; a receipts question is usually "After" or "Completion"; a check the person would only sometimes want is "On demand".
- paradigm is decided per widget, by what the finding is, and is independent of the cluster. The same cluster can take different paradigms: two facts questions can be paradigm 5 and paradigm 6 depending on whether the point is the page's exact words or that the value moved.
- the widget "template" is one or two spoken sentences, in quotes, with {0} {1} slots where live page values go. it talks like a person, not a system: "Stop. The price went up. You approved {0}. It is now {1}."
- "needs" lists the page facts the widget has to read before it can say its line, as short field names in the exemplar's style ("resultCount", "priceNow", "fareRules"). The number of names in "needs" must equal the number of {n} slots in the template, or the widget can never fire.
- "control" is what the user can do about it. "label" is the affirmative option and "decline" is the way to wave it off - both from the type's option pair on its card, or a sharper task-specific wording of the same pair. "action" is the type's standing slug: refine-narrow, compare-diff, facts-source, photos-describe, receipts-readback, approve-change, undo-last, watch-track, or hand-over. When the widget hands the user the actual page control instead, slugify the question for the action (like "can-you-pick-the-size") and add "hands": a short phrase saying what they get to do.
- the widget "name" is two to four words that say the widget's move ("Price change gate", "Count-first opener").

Here is the model - task, ask, and its tree with questions:

<<MODEL>>

Code exactly these questions, all of them:

Each line below is `id | where it sits in the task | question`. Where it
sits decides the moment and decides whether continuing past it is hard to
undo - a question under a checkout or a submit step usually is, one under a
search step usually is not.

<<SCOPE>>

Answer with only JSON, no prose around it:
{"codings": [{"nodeId": "...", "question": "the exact question text", "cluster": "...", "moment": "...", "paradigm": 7, "moneyMoving": false, "costDims": {"money": 0, "privacy": 0, "thirdParty": 0, "safety": 0, "reversibility": 0, "recovery": 0}, "exampleWidgets": [{"name": "...", "template": "...", "needs": ["..."], "control": {"label": "...", "action": "...", "decline": "..."}}]}],
 "newTypeCards": []}

"paradigm" is an integer from 1 to 12. Every coding must carry one.

"moneyMoving" is true when backing out from here would cost something rather than
just needing a click. The test is: if the person changed their mind at this step,
could they simply navigate away, or would they have to cancel, refund, unfile or
re-submit something?

  - Filling in a name, picking a seat, choosing a fare, reading terms: you can walk
    away from all of these and nothing has happened. FALSE.
  - But "walk away" means the world is unchanged, not that you personally left.
    Putting goods into a basket or cart that is still holding them when you come
    back has already changed something, and every check from there on is inside
    the commitment window. This is why the shopping task marks over half its
    questions true and starts doing so at the cart, not at the payment.
  - A part-filled form is NOT this. A draft application, a form you have started
    but not filed, and a search you have not run are all still nothing: you can
    close the tab and the world is as it was. The form task marks fewer than a
    fifth of its questions true, and only around filing and what follows it.
  - Submitting the payment, filing the form, confirming the booking, and every check
    that reads back what was just committed: FALSE is not available here. TRUE.

"costDims" grades what an UNDETECTED error at this check would cost the person,
six integers 0 to 3 each (0 none, 1 low, 2 medium, 3 high), judged for THIS task:

  - "money": money at stake if this check is wrong. A rate or total: 2-3. A
    filter or sort order that only wastes a search: 0-1.
  - "privacy": privacy or identity exposure. Wrong account or profile, data
    shared beyond intent.
  - "thirdParty": something reaches a real person in the user's name - a
    message sent, money moved to someone, a booking under an identity.
  - "safety": safety or legal consequence - medication, legal filing,
    anything with rules attached.
  - "reversibility": how hard the consequence is to reverse. Navigating away
    fixes it: 0. Cancel or refund flow: 2. Effectively permanent (sent
    message, filed form, shared data): 3.
  - "recovery": effort to notice the error later and redo the work, even
    when reversal is possible.

Code the dimensions independently - most questions are 0 on most dimensions,
and a question can be high on one and zero on the rest. Do not let moneyMoving
leak into every dimension: moneyMoving is about the STEP being a commitment;
costDims is about the ERROR this particular question would let through.

So it clusters tightly around the commit itself and the confirmation after it, not
across the whole flow that leads up to it. In the human-built flights model it is
about a fifth of all questions; in the shopping model, where the cart itself is a
commitment, about half; in the research model, none at all. If you are marking most
of a task true, you are marking the run-up rather than the commitment.

Each entry in "newTypeCards", if you truly need one: {"name": "...", "whatItIs": "...", "whenItApplies": "...", "options": "affirmative / decline", "example": "...", "whyNoneOfTheNineFit": "..."}
strong-paradigm-cards:
# The twelve paradigms

The interface type decides what options the person gets. The paradigm decides the shape the
widget draws. They are different axes and a question needs both: a question with a type but no
paradigm can be spoken and cannot be drawn.

Pick exactly one number, 1 to 12, per widget. Pick by what the finding *is*, not by the type.

| n | name | shape | pick it when the finding is |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The glance, translated | gauge | one quantity whose size is the whole point - a result count, a share that is sponsored, a total against a limit the person set |
| 2 | Claim vs evidence | triangulation | whether two or more independent sources agree about one claim - the spec table, a photo, a review, all asked the same thing |
| 3 | Diff against the ask | literal diff | how what the page says lines up, row by row, with what the person actually asked for |
| 4 | What I didn't look at | coverage map | the size of what was skipped - how many reviews went unread, how many photos unopened, how many options unchecked |
| 5 | Poke the world | magnifier | the page's exact wording, quoted live, with where on the page it sits and when it was read |
| 6 | Time-stamped world | timeline | that a value moved, or that a value is older than it looks - the same field at several times |
| 7 | The airlock | chamber | a held gate before something hard to undo, reading back every fact about the commit while nothing has happened yet |
| 8 | Rules from corrections | switchboard | that a standing rule the person set has fired, or is about to be broken |
| 9 | The auditor | (falls back to the sentence) | a check made against a source the agent did not write - a confirmation email, an account page, a saved address |
| 10 | The escort | numbered path | steps the person has to take with their own hands, in order, because the agent cannot or must not press them |
| 11 | The world, rebuilt | funnel | a long screen compressed into one sentence the person can hold |
| 12 | The road not taken | fork | what was chosen against what was passed over, stated in the same fields so the two can be compared |

Worked examples, all from the Amazon model:

- paradigm 1, "6 of the first 10 results are ads." - read off 10 tiles, 6 carrying a Sponsored label.
- paradigm 2, "Two sources agree: the strap is real. The spec table and photo 3."
- paradigm 3, "Your words: strap on the back. The page: Adjustable Velcro Straps. Not the same yet."
- paradigm 4, "Before you decide: I did not read any reviews. 84 exist."
- paradigm 5, "Checking the tile you named. The word Sponsored sits directly above its title."
- paradigm 6, "$12.93, read just now. This sandal has also shown $12.60 and $15.10."
- paradigm 7, "Ready to buy. Nothing pressed. Total $16.52. Say 'place it' to spend the money."
- paradigm 8, "$48.20 order. Over your $25 limit. I stopped."
- paradigm 9, "Address on the order: David Lin, San Jose. Matches your saved home address."
- paradigm 10, "I can't press cancel myself. I'll walk you to it."
- paradigm 11, "3 items, $44.06. Your new sandals at $15.10, plus two older items at $28.96."
- paradigm 12, "Your sandal: 4.0 stars from 84. The best one passed over: 4.6 from 2,624."
type-cards:
# Interface type cards

These are the ten interface types: nine from the Amazon analysis (deck/decisions.html), and watch, admitted 2026-08-08 from the flights gold videos under the new-types rule below. Each validation question in a task model gets exactly one type. The type decides what the widget looks like and what options the user gets.

The vocabulary is open but not free. A generated task model should use these ten types wherever they fit. It can propose a new type only by writing a full card in this same format - a definition, when it applies, the option pair, and a worked example - plus one sentence on why none of the nine fit. A proposed type that cannot fill out the card gets rejected during scoring.

The moment (Now, After, Completion, On demand) is coded separately from the type. For example, an approve question is usually Now (pause the agent) while a receipts question is usually Completion, but the pairing is decided per question, not per type.

---

## refine

**What it is.** The user reacts to the size or makeup of a result set and decides whether to cut it down before anything gets picked from it. For example, when doing a search, the user will first react to the total number of results and determine which ones are sponsored results vs. actual top results.

**When it applies.** Any point where a query, filter, or sort produced a set that is about to be worked from. The question is about the set, not about any single item in it.

**The options.** Narrow it down / Keep them all.

**Example from Amazon.** "How many results?" - the search returned over 9,000 results. The widget reads the count with its source line ("1-48 of over 9,000 results for"), and narrowing means trying more specific search words. With the probe, the narrower options carry real measured counts instead of estimates.

## compare

**What it is.** The user weighs several candidates against each other on the same dimensions - price, rating, appearance - before taking one seriously.

**When it applies.** A page shows multiple candidates side by side, or the agent has looked at several and is about to pick. The question is about differences, so the widget leads with the dimension where the candidates differ most.

**The options.** Read me the differences / Fine as is.

**Example from Amazon.** "How are they rated?" - stars and review counts across the visible tiles. A sighted person gets this in one glance across the grid; the widget has to say it, so it says the widest gap first (e.g., "they differ most on rating") instead of reading every tile.

## select

**What it is.** The user picks one option from a set the interface offers - a size, a color, a delivery speed. The set is the page's, not the user's, so the first job is telling the user what the options even are.

**When it applies.** The page has a control with enumerable choices and the choice belongs to the user, not the agent. In the recorded runs, the agent picking a size on its own is exactly the moment that needed a hold.

**The options.** Read me the options / You pick.

**Example from Amazon.** "Can you pick the size?" - the size selector lists 5, 5 Big Kid, 6. The ask said size 5, the page preselected 5 Big Kid, and the difference is a real decision only the user can make.

## approve

**What it is.** The user gives or withholds a go-ahead before a step that commits something - adding to cart, checking out, placing the order. This is the type that pauses the agent, because after the step there is no free moment left to object.

**When it applies.** The next action changes something that is tedious or impossible to take back. The widget reads back exactly what is about to happen (the item, the total, the card, the address) before the step runs, not after.

**The options.** Hold on, check it with me / Go ahead.

**Example from Amazon.** "Can you place it?" - the standing rule "never press place your order yourself" is this type written down as a rule. The widget reads the order facts one by one before the user confirms.

## facts

**What it is.** The user checks a claim against what the page actually says. The widget's job is to read out the page's own words, so the user can check where the claim came from.

**When it applies.** Something the ask depends on is stated somewhere on the page (a price, a stock line, a spec, a review), and the user needs it read out with its source, not summarized.

**The options.** Read me where it says that / Got it.

**Example from Amazon.** "Is size 5 in stock?" - the stock line says "Only 3 left in stock". The widget quotes it verbatim, so the user hears what the page says instead of the agent's account of it.

## photos

**What it is.** The user needs what is only in the pictures. For a BVI user this information is gone at every automation level without a describer - the screen reader just says "graphic" for each photo.

**When it applies.** A visual property matters to the decision (does the strap go behind the heel, does the color match) and the listing text does not state it.

**The options.** Describe the photos / Got it.

**Example from Amazon.** "Do photos prove it?" - the ask requires a strap behind the heel. The text never says it; one product photo shows it. The describer checks the claim against both sources: the photo confirms the strap, and the text never mentions it.

## receipts

**What it is.** The user gets a record of what actually happened - the confirmation the interface showed briefly and then replaced. For example, after adding to cart, the page shows "Added to cart" briefly and the user needs that kept somewhere they can go back to.

**When it applies.** A step claims to have worked, and the evidence is transient (a toast, a count ticking up, a confirmation page that will be navigated away from). The widget captures the evidence at the moment it exists.

**The options.** Read it back to me / Got it.

**Example from Amazon.** "Which size went in?" - the cart line says the size that actually went in, which is what tells the user whether the add worked with the right variant. The order number and confirmation email are the same type at Completion.

## undo

**What it is.** The user takes something back - removes the extra item, cancels the order inside its cancel window. The widget's job is to say how to reverse the step and by when, because most reversal paths expire.

**When it applies.** A committed step has a reversal path (cancel, return, remove) and the path has conditions or a time limit worth saying out loud.

**The options.** Undo it / Leave it.

**Example from Amazon.** "Can you cancel it?" - after placing the order there is a short window where cancelling is one click. "Free returns?" is the same type asked earlier, before the user commits to the order.

## hand over

**What it is.** The agent gives one control back to the user - a field to type in, an error to resolve - and then continues the run. Some steps are the user's by nature, e.g., entering a password or fixing a form error the agent caused.

**When it applies.** The step needs information or judgment only the user has, or the interface is refusing the agent (a login wall, a CAPTCHA, a validation error).

**The options.** Let me do this part / Carry on.

**Example from Amazon.** "Any form errors?" - a checkout field error appears in red and clears silently. The widget hands the user that one field with the error text, then the agent continues from the corrected state.

## watch

**What it is.** The user sets the system to monitor a changing value - a price, an availability - and report movements, instead of deciding now. It converts a decision the user is not ready to make into a standing alert: the interface keeps looking so the user can stop.

**When it applies.** A value the decision depends on fluctuates over time, and the user either is not ready to commit or has already committed but the value can still be re-contested (a fare drop within a rebookable fare class). It is not a one-time read of the page (facts), not a cut of the current result set (refine), and not a reversal of anything (undo) - the defining move is delegating attention across time.

**The options.** Watch it for me / Decide now.

**Example from the flights gold.** Google Flights "Track prices": the expert judges the fares too expensive, declines to book, and toggles the tracker - the page confirms "You'll get emails when prices change" (video dM5AoLocriM, 13:32). The same expert keeps the watch on after booking, because a later drop means cancel and rebook. Four of the six flights videos use this move.
